title: EPA Rescinds Methane Standards for Oil and Gas Operations in 2020
description_medium: On August 13, 2020, the Environmental Protection Agency issued a final policy rule removing the transmission and storage segment from federal oil-and-gas emissions standards and rescinding methane standards for production and processing segments. The EPA said the changes reduced compliance burdens. Congress later disapproved the policy rule in 2021, ending its effect.
description_long: On August 13, 2020, the Environmental Protection Agency finalized policy and technical amendments to its New Source Performance Standards for the oil and natural gas industry. The policy rule removed transmission and storage operations from the covered segment and rescinded methane and volatile-organic-compound standards for that segment. It also removed methane-specific standards for production and processing operations. EPA said the changes would simplify compliance and reduce costs for the industry, arguing that controls for volatile organic compounds also reduced methane and that federal requirements overlapped with other regulation. Environmental groups and some states criticized the rollback as weakening controls on methane, a potent greenhouse gas. The separate technical rule adjusted monitoring, repair, recordkeeping and reporting provisions. The distinction between those two rules matters because the policy amendments removed emissions standards, while the technical package modified implementation details. Congress later passed a Congressional Review Act resolution disapproving the 2020 policy rule, signed into law on June 30, 2021; EPA states the policy amendments were no longer in effect after that date. The entry describes the policy action at the time it was adopted, while noting that Congress subsequently overturned it.
source_access_notes: Read EPA’s event-specific final-rule summary and its August 2020 announcement; EPA’s page also records Congress’s 2021 disapproval and effective status.
rationale: Replaces the unrelated 2026 BBC link with EPA’s primary source and distinguishes the emissions-standard rollback from technical amendments and the later CRA reversal.

title: White House Physician Ronny Jackson Calls Trump’s Health ‘Excellent’ After Physical
description_medium: After Donald Trump’s January 2018 physical, White House physician Ronny Jackson told reporters that the 71-year-old president was in “excellent” health and fit for duty. Jackson reported a perfect 30/30 score on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment and described Trump’s cardiac health as strong, while advising him to lose 10 to 15 pounds and lower his LDL cholesterol. Jackson attributed the president’s stamina partly to “incredible genes.”
description_long: White House physician Ronny Jackson briefed reporters on January 16, 2018, after examining President Donald Trump at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center. Jackson called Trump’s overall health “excellent” and said clinical data supported his being fit for duty. He reported that Trump scored 30 out of 30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, a screening test for serious cognitive impairment. Jackson also described Trump’s cardiac health favorably, but said the president should lose 10 to 15 pounds and lower his LDL cholesterol; Trump was 6 feet 3 inches tall and weighed 239 pounds, which CBS described as borderline obese. When asked how Trump remained healthy despite limited exercise and a fast-food diet, Jackson pointed to what he called the president’s “incredible genes.” Those remarks were the physician’s assessment, not independent proof that Trump had exceptional genetics or would remain healthy for many years. The press briefing made the White House’s health disclosure unusually expansive by addressing physical fitness, cognition, diet and future capacity for office. This account focuses on Jackson’s reported examination findings and advice, rather than extending the story to unrelated later controversies involving him.
source_access_notes: Read the linked CBS report; it contains Jackson’s statements, the cognitive-screen result, weight and cholesterol advice, and his ‘incredible genes’ remark.
rationale: Removes unsupported editorial and unrelated later allegations while retaining the specific claims and medical advice reported from Jackson’s briefing.

title: Trump Warns North Korea of “Fire and Fury” if It Threatens the United States
description_medium: On August 8, 2017, President Donald Trump warned that North Korea would face “fire and fury like the world has never seen” if it threatened the United States. Reuters reported the remark amid escalating threats between Washington and Pyongyang. The statement was made to reporters, not in the separate January 2018 tweet about Trump’s “nuclear button.”
description_long: As tensions with North Korea rose in August 2017, President Donald Trump told reporters that the country would face “fire and fury like the world has never seen” if it threatened the United States. Reuters reported the warning on August 8, after Pyongyang issued threats connected to its nuclear and missile programs. Trump’s phrase became part of a broader exchange of increasingly combative public statements between the two governments. The cited Reuters report covers this verbal warning; it does not describe Trump issuing a tweet or declaring that he would launch a nuclear attack. A separate post from January 2018 responded to North Korean leader Kim Jong Un’s claim that a nuclear button was on his desk, with Trump boasting that his own button was “much bigger and more powerful.” The two statements occurred months apart and should not be merged into a single event. The August remark supports an account of Trump’s public warning and the heightened rhetoric at the time. The title has been narrowed accordingly; the available event-specific record does not identify a matching August tweet or substantiate a literal threat to begin nuclear war.

corrected_wording.title: Trump Warns North Korea of “Fire and Fury” if It Threatens the United States
corrected_wording.description: Reuters reports the August 2017 remark to reporters; the nuclear-button tweet was a separate statement in January 2018.

source_access_notes: Read the linked Reuters account of the August 2017 statement and contemporaneous reporting on the distinct January 2018 nuclear-button tweet.
blockers: The linked August Reuters story documents a spoken warning, not the Twitter nuclear-button claim named in the original headline.
rationale: Separates the August 2017 ‘fire and fury’ statement from the January 2018 tweet and removes the unsupported claim that this event was a Twitter threat of nuclear war.

title: EPA Denies Petition to Ban Chlorpyrifos in March 2017
description_medium: On March 29, 2017, EPA Administrator Scott Pruitt denied a petition by the Natural Resources Defense Council and Pesticide Action Network North America to revoke food-residue tolerances for chlorpyrifos. The decision left the pesticide’s registered uses available while EPA continued its broader review. EPA cited concerns about the science used in the earlier proposed ban; the Ninth Circuit later found the denial arbitrary and capricious and ordered the agency to act again.
description_long: On March 29, 2017, Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Scott Pruitt denied a petition seeking to revoke all food-residue tolerances for chlorpyrifos, an insecticide used on crops. The petition had been filed by the Natural Resources Defense Council and Pesticide Action Network North America. The EPA’s announcement said the agency rejected the prior administration’s proposed ban, citing concerns about the epidemiological studies used to support it and objections raised by a federal pesticide-science advisory panel. The denial kept chlorpyrifos tolerances in place at that point; it did not resolve the chemical’s safety debate. The groups challenged the decision, and in 2021 the Ninth Circuit held that EPA’s denial was arbitrary and capricious on the record before the court. The court directed EPA to grant the petition and issue a final rule either revoking the tolerances or modifying them if EPA could support a safety determination. The later ruling provides important context, but the event recorded here is the 2017 decision. The case shows the conflict between EPA’s stated reliance on scientific uncertainty and the court’s conclusion that the agency had not lawfully answered the petition. EPA’s chronology reflects that subsequent regulatory actions followed the court order.
source_access_notes: The supplied EPA URL was dead, so I located and read EPA’s archived March 29, 2017 release and its current chlorpyrifos chronology, which records the Ninth Circuit’s later ruling.
rationale: Restores the accurate petitioners, date and agency rationale from EPA’s archived release and adds the consequential 2021 court ruling with its procedural scope.

title: BLM Approves Oil and Gas Leasing Program for ANWR Coastal Plain
description_medium: On August 17, 2020, Interior Secretary David Bernhardt approved a Record of Decision for oil and gas leasing across the 1.56-million-acre Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. The decision made the program area available for future lease sales, as required by the 2017 tax law. BLM described lease stipulations and operating procedures intended to protect surface resources and subsistence use.
description_long: On August 17, 2020, Interior Secretary David Bernhardt signed a Record of Decision approving the Coastal Plain Oil and Gas Leasing Program in Alaska’s Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. The decision made approximately 1.56 million acres available for leasing and specified where and under what terms leasing could occur. Congress had directed at least two area-wide lease sales of no fewer than 400,000 acres each in the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act. BLM said the approved program included lease stipulations and required operating procedures addressing surface resources and subsistence use. The decision applied to the Coastal Plain, about eight percent of the 19.3-million-acre refuge; it did not open the entire refuge to oil and gas development. The Record of Decision completed the federal environmental review step for the program, after BLM considered public comments and analyzed alternatives in an environmental impact statement. Approval created the framework for lease sales and possible later exploration and development, rather than authorizing immediate drilling across every parcel. The record therefore marks an administrative and land-use decision with potential consequences for a protected Arctic landscape and the communities and wildlife that depend on it. Subsequent lease and permitting steps remained necessary before production could begin.
source_access_notes: Read BLM’s August 17, 2020 decision announcement and program page; they identify the 1.56-million-acre area, statutory lease-sale direction and surface-use protections.
rationale: Adds the acreage, statutory basis and scope of the ROD while distinguishing program approval from later leasing and drilling.

title: BLM Revises Methane Waste Rule, Rescinding Equipment Leak Requirements
description_medium: On September 18, 2018, the Bureau of Land Management finalized revisions to its 2016 Waste Prevention Rule for oil and gas operations on federal and tribal lands. The rule removed prescriptive requirements for pneumatic equipment, storage tanks and leak detection and repair, while retaining time or volume limits on some royalty-free venting and flaring. Interior said the revision reduced compliance burdens and restored longstanding requirements.
description_long: The Bureau of Land Management finalized revisions to its 2016 Waste Prevention Rule, also known as the Venting and Flaring Rule, on September 18, 2018. The earlier rule addressed natural gas lost through venting, flaring and leaks on federal and tribal lands. The Trump-era revision removed prescriptive requirements for pneumatic equipment, storage tanks and leak detection and repair, and eliminated several associated planning and reporting requirements. BLM said the 2016 requirements overlapped with state, tribal and federal regulation and imposed costs it considered excessive. The revised rule retained limits on royalty-free venting and flaring during production testing, emergencies and well maintenance, and kept provisions allowing gas used in operations to be royalty-free. The result was a narrower federal mandate for operators to install specific equipment and monitor leaks, alongside continued restrictions on certain waste practices. Environmental advocates argued that loosening mandatory controls could increase methane emissions, while Interior presented the revisions as a way to reduce compliance burdens and preserve operator flexibility. This account identifies the specific requirements changed rather than implying every methane or waste rule was eliminated. The action changed federal requirements for public-land oil and gas operations; its environmental effects depend on industry practice and other applicable rules.
source_access_notes: Replaced the unrelated Facebook link with the Department of Interior announcement and the BLM final rule; read both to identify rescinded leak, tank and pneumatic-equipment requirements.
rationale: Clarifies which 2016 controls the 2018 final rule removed and which venting/flaring limits remained, rather than claiming the whole rule disappeared.

title: EPA Amends Coal Ash Disposal Rules, Adding Flexibility for Utilities and States
description_medium: On July 18, 2018, EPA finalized the first revisions to its 2015 coal-combustion-residuals rules. The amendments gave states and utilities more flexibility in managing coal ash, including tailoring requirements to site-specific risks; EPA estimated annual regulatory-cost savings of $28 million to $31 million. The entry concerns the 2018 amendments, not the distinct 2024 rule that expanded requirements for legacy ash sites.
description_long: On July 18, 2018, the Environmental Protection Agency finalized the first set of revisions to its 2015 regulations for coal combustion residuals, commonly called coal ash. The rules govern disposal at coal-fired power plants, including landfills and surface impoundments where ash can pose risks through leaks, dust and structural failures. EPA said the revisions gave utilities and states added flexibility to manage coal ash and allowed requirements to be tailored to site-specific risk considerations. The agency estimated that the changes would save $28 million to $31 million a year in regulatory costs. EPA framed the amendments as reducing burdens while continuing to protect health and the environment; critics viewed the changes as weakening aspects of the federal safeguards. The 2018 amendments followed a court decision and stakeholder comments on the original rule. They are separate from EPA’s 2024 rule covering legacy ash impoundments at inactive facilities, which expanded federal coverage in response to another court ruling. The event’s core is a Trump-era revision of the coal-ash disposal framework, and its policy tradeoff involved compliance flexibility and cost savings versus uniform federal requirements. The cited EPA release provides the agency’s description and cost estimate, but not independent measurements of resulting pollution or health impacts.
source_access_notes: Located and read EPA’s archived July 18, 2018 release for the date-matched event; excluded the supplied 2024 rule, which concerned a different action and strengthened legacy-site coverage.
rationale: Matches the entry’s July 2018 date to EPA’s actual 2018 amendments and replaces the misleading 2024-source interpretation with the event’s reported flexibilities and savings estimate.

title: Treasury Lifts Sanctions on Three Deripaska-Linked Companies, Not Deripaska
description_medium: On January 27, 2019, Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control removed En+, Rusal and EuroSibEnergo from the sanctions list after the companies reduced Oleg Deripaska’s ownership stakes and severed his control, Treasury said. Deripaska himself remained sanctioned. The decision followed a congressional review and objections from lawmakers who argued that his influence over the companies might continue.
description_long: On January 27, 2019, the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control lifted sanctions on three companies linked to Russian businessman Oleg Deripaska: En+, aluminum producer Rusal and EuroSibEnergo. Treasury said the companies had reduced Deripaska’s direct and indirect shareholdings and severed his control, and that independent directors would form a majority of the En+ and Rusal boards. The action followed Treasury’s December 2018 notification to Congress and a debate in which lawmakers sought to block the delisting. The sanctions removal applied to the three corporate entities; it did not remove Deripaska from the U.S. sanctions list. Treasury maintained restrictions on him personally. The distinction is important because the original headline suggests sanctions on Deripaska himself were lifted along with those on his aluminum company. Treasury presented the restructuring as sufficient to separate the companies from his control, while critics questioned whether the changes would fully limit his influence. The official release establishes the administration’s stated basis and the companies affected, but it does not resolve the political dispute over the adequacy of the ownership and governance changes. The event was a sanctions-policy decision involving major Russian businesses and a prominent oligarch, rather than a direct delisting of Deripaska.

corrected_wording.title: Treasury Lifts Sanctions on Three Deripaska-Linked Companies, Not Deripaska
corrected_wording.description: Treasury’s action removed En+, Rusal and EuroSibEnergo from the sanctions list; Deripaska’s personal designation remained.

source_access_notes: Read Treasury’s January 27 release; it names the three delisted companies and says Deripaska’s stakes and control were reduced, while his own listing was not removed.
rationale: Corrects the original conflation of corporate delisting with removal of Deripaska’s personal sanctions and adds Treasury’s stated conditions.

title: Trump Commutes Sentences of Seditious-Conspiracy Leaders and Pardons Other Jan. 6 Defendants
description_medium: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump commuted the sentences of 14 January 6 defendants, including Oath Keepers leader Kelly Meggs and Proud Boys leaders Joseph Biggs and Zachary Rehl, all convicted of seditious conspiracy. The proclamation granted full pardons to other people convicted of January 6-related offenses and directed the Justice Department to dismiss pending indictments. It did not pardon the three named leaders; their sentences were commuted to time served.
description_long: President Donald Trump issued a clemency proclamation on January 20, 2025, covering federal offenses related to the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol. It commuted the sentences of 14 named defendants to time served, including Oath Keepers leader Kelly Meggs and Proud Boys members Joseph Biggs and Zachary Rehl, each convicted of seditious conspiracy. The proclamation granted a full, complete and unconditional pardon to all other people convicted of January 6-related offenses and directed the attorney general to seek dismissal with prejudice of pending indictments tied to the events. The legal distinction matters: Meggs, Biggs and Rehl received commutations, which ended their remaining prison sentences, while the proclamation pardoned the other convicted defendants. The action did not spare all members of the two organizations from prosecution based on unrelated conduct, but it extended clemency to the covered January 6 offenses and directed dismissal of pending cases over that conduct. The original headline’s broad “pardons leaders” wording obscures the different forms of relief. The official proclamation names the commuted defendants and defines the scope of the pardon and dismissal directives. It documents a sweeping change in federal accountability for January 6 offenses, while leaving separate state cases and unrelated criminal matters outside its stated terms.

corrected_wording.title: Trump Commutes Sentences of Seditious-Conspiracy Leaders and Pardons Other Jan. 6 Defendants
corrected_wording.description: The proclamation commuted sentences for Meggs, Biggs and Rehl, and pardoned all other convicted defendants covered by its terms.

source_access_notes: Read the official January 20 proclamation and DOJ’s clemency page; the proclamation explicitly lists the 14 commutations, including Meggs, Biggs and Rehl, and separately pardons the remaining convicted defendants.
rationale: Corrects the conflation of commutation and pardon and names the covered relief precisely from the presidential proclamation.

title: Trump Signs Law Repealing FCC Broadband Privacy Rules
description_medium: President Donald Trump signed Public Law 115-22 on April 3, 2017, disapproving the FCC’s broadband privacy rule. The repealed rule would have required internet service providers to obtain customer consent before using or sharing certain sensitive information, including browsing data. The law also barred the FCC from issuing a substantially similar rule under the Congressional Review Act; the FCC later said broadband privacy jurisdiction returned to the FTC.
description_long: On April 3, 2017, President Donald Trump signed Senate Joint Resolution 34, enacted as Public Law 115-22, under the Congressional Review Act. The law disapproved the Federal Communications Commission’s 2016 rule titled “Protecting the Privacy of Customers of Broadband and Other Telecommunications Services.” That rule would have required internet service providers to obtain customer consent before using or sharing sensitive information such as browsing history, app usage and precise geolocation. The resolution nullified the FCC rule and, under the Congressional Review Act, prevented the agency from issuing a substantially similar rule without new statutory authorization. The FCC subsequently said that restoring broadband to an information-service classification returned privacy and data-security oversight to the Federal Trade Commission, which had regulated providers before the FCC’s 2015 reclassification. The policy change therefore altered which agency had authority and removed the FCC’s specific opt-in framework for broadband providers. It did not make all collection or sale of customer information lawful without limits; other consumer-protection authorities and laws continued to apply. The original short description’s broad statement that the rules simply barred providers from selling browsing data lacks the nuance of the rule’s consent and information-use provisions. This account identifies the law and its institutional effect without implying that every privacy protection disappeared.

corrected_wording.title: Trump Signs Law Repealing FCC Broadband Privacy Rules
corrected_wording.description: Public Law 115-22 nullified the 2016 FCC rule and restricted the FCC from adopting a substantially similar rule under the CRA.

source_access_notes: Read the GovInfo record for Public Law 115-22 and the FCC’s subsequent Restoring Internet Freedom order describing the jurisdictional effect; the CNBC article linked in the packet was not needed.
rationale: Identifies the statute, what FCC rule it nullified and the later jurisdictional consequence, correcting the oversimplified description of browsing-data sales.
